messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

Please forgive my ignorance as I am very much a novice when it comes to using R and performing distance sampling analysis.

Firstly, can anyone help me with model selection when all AIC values are very similar - should the lowest AIC value model always be selected if Goodness of Fit for all models are also similarly desirable? When plotting and selecting the best model does shoulder width and the value of the endpoint of the line also come into consideration?

These are the following AIC values I obtained from my data of 357 observations total.

Half-normal cosine                            AIC: 3154.2                         AIC: 2872.3                   AIC: 2646
Half-normal hermite polynomial        AIC: 3154.2                         AIC: 2872.3                   AIC: 2646
Uniform cosine                                  AIC: 3152                            AIC: 2871.6                   AIC: 2644.4
Hazard-rate simple polynomial         AIC: 3163.7                         AIC: 2873.3                   AIC: 2646.8

The following plots of my data are all truncated at 5% using the following models: hazard rate with simple polynomial, half-normal cosine and uniform cosine. BAsed on this information if I decided to go with a 5% truncated model, should the uniform cosine model be selected because it has the lowest AIC value?

Secondly, how do I interpret some of the summary data values? What does Average P mean and how should the associated average P values be interpreted? I have included an example of the summary data for one of the models below.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Importing the data into DISTANCE: transects with no observations
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Importing the data into DISTANCE: transects with no observations
messages.body_plain:
Margherita

If you have no sightings on a transect, the information about that transect (its ID and its length) must still be imported into Distance--as you say it is only the perpendicular distance and cluster size that can remain blank.  However placeholders must be left for those blank fields.

Here is an example

To import a data file into Distance, it must be in "flat file format" - i.e., arranged in rows and columns with one row for each observation. The actual number of columns depends on the type of survey (see later). Here's an example of part of a data file, from a line transect survey with two strata:

Stratum 1;100;Line 1;10;14
Stratum 1;100;Line 1;10;8
Stratum 1;100;Line 1;10;22
Stratum 1;100;Line 2;10.3;7
Stratum 1;100;Line 2;10.3;37
Stratum 1;100;Line 2;10.3;13
Stratum 2;123;Line 1;5.7;
Stratum 2;123;Line 2;8.4;27
Stratum 2;123;Line 2;8.4;76
Stratum 2;123;Line 2;8.4;44
Stratum 2;123;Line 2;8.4;7

In this file, the columns are separated by semicolons. Column 1 is the stratum name, column 2 is the stratum area, column 3 is the transect name, column 4 is the transect length, and column 5 is the perpendicular distance. Notice that all transects from the same stratum are grouped together on adjacent lines, and all observations from the same transect are grouped together. Notice also that the record "Line 1" in "Stratum 2" has no distance in the final column - this is a transect where no objects were seen.

This example does not have cluster size, simply perpendicular distance.  If there was cluster size, you would have two semicolons in succession for Stratum 2, Line 1 where there were no detections.

If this still does not answer your question, send me your data (off list) and I will look at it.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Model selection and interpreting summary data
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Model selection and interpreting summary data
messages.body_plain:
Luke

Apologies for the delayed response.

A couple of general comments about model selection in relation to distance sampling.  It is usually the case that for data collected conscientiously (therefore containing a reasonable shoulder--drop off in detections is not too sudden; no evidence of rounding of distances to favoured values; good sample sizes) there may be little difference in fit between key function models half-normal and hazard rate.  The histograms you sent along suggests your data are reasonably good.

You note that the difference in AIC values among the models you fitted is small with modest truncation.  Conventional wisdom suggests there is little evidence to support one model over another if AIC<2 (as is the case with your 5 and 10% truncation).  Hence your decision process then moves to the absolute measures of fit (goodness of fit tests) and if they indicate good fit of both candidate models, you are still unconstrained in choosing between models.  The uniform key with cosine adjustment is also known as the Fourier series model and it is know to perform well.  You will notice the shape of the fitted uniform cosine and the fitted half-normal cosine are nearly identical; particularly at small distances.  This suggests that the inference drawn from both models will be nearly identical.

Moral of the story, when you have decent data several models will fit those data equally well and model selection is not a cause for concern.

Your second question about the "p" reported in output from the function ds().  This is interpreted as the probability of an individual inside the truncation distance being detected.  It is the ratio of area under the fitted detection function to the area under a rectangle of height 1 out to the truncation distance.  It is the quantity by which the number of detections is divided to produce the other quantity in the output: "N in covered region".  In your case you had 339 detections after truncation; dividing 339 by 0.622 results in the estimate of "N in covered region" of 545.

I hope this is useful.

messages.subject: Density estimation in R with multiple covariates
messages.subject_clean: Density estimation in R with multiple covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I want to get density estimates for individual species from a multi-year bird survey (line transects), using year, observer, and cluster size as covariates as I have reason to believe that each might affect a species' detectability.  Ultimately, I would like to run the model: ds(data, ... , cutpoints = c(0,15,35,55,75,105,145), ... , formula = ~ as.factor(year) + as.factor(observer) + size).

Year
I think that year is affecting species' detectability because when I plotted detection function for each species with year as a covariate to see whether detection functions were different in each year and found that for many species the shape of the detection function was markedly different. However, this could be an artefact of having different observers in each year. I chose to use year as a covariate rather than doing full stratification by year (i.e. getting a separate detection function for each year) because the latter approach greatly limited the number of species with sufficient number observations (60 observations per stratum).

Observer
I have five years of data, and in each year two to three different teams conducted surveys, with essentially no overlap between teams in different years, giving 12 unique observer team IDs. Differences is observer effort and skill level can obviously lead to different biases in how species are detected, so I'd like to account for that.

Cluster size
I used cluster size as a covariate because I want to account for cluster-size bias (larger flock sizes are more likely to be detected at further distances).

Problems:

1.) I am able to run ds models when my flatfile contains year as the only covariate (with columns 'Region.Label', 'Area', 'Sample.Label', 'Effort', 'distance', 'size', 'year', and 'species'). When I add an 'observer' column to my flatfile (with columns 'Region.Label', 'Area', 'Sample.Label', 'Effort', 'observer', 'distance', 'size', 'year', and 'species') and run the same model (with year as the only covariate), I get errors saying all models failed to fit/no models could be fitted. This tells me that adding an 'observer' column somehow messes up the flatfile and I cannot figure why this might be. I'd appreciate any ideas!

2.) Also, how should I assess model fit? I am using manually defined cutpoints/bins (6 in total) because of heaping of 'exact' distance estimates, and when year is used as a covariate there are 5 levels (2012-2016) so there are no remaining degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness of fit test.

Thanks very much,
Michelle

messages.subject: binning data for MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Thanks in advance for any responses. I've developed most of my models so far in Program Distance to explore possible models. From these models I've concluded that a MCDS using a hazard-rate key and observer as a covariate for detection with a set of manual intervals and distance data truncated to 105 meters, is likely to be my best model. However I now want to try playing around with that model in R and am trying to reconstruct it using the ddf() function, but keep running into a small error. I found some of the examples from distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org> to be very useful and have used them to help  guide this, but keep running into problems with the distbegin/end arguements. Here's a copy of my code so far:

SHCR <- pt_cnts_distance_2016_v4
SHCR$Observer_init <- factor(SHCR$Observer_init)

SHCR.fixed <- Distance:::checkdata(SHCR)
SHCR.fixed$distbegin = 0
SHCR.fixed$distend = 105
SHCR.ddf <- ddf(method = 'ds', dsmodel = ~mcds(key = 'hr', formula=~Observer_init), data = SHCR.fixed$data,
                meta.data = list(point = TRUE, binned = TRUE, breaks = c(0,20,40,60,80,105)))
Error in process.data(data, meta.data, check = FALSE) :
  binned set to TRUE in meta.data but distbegin and distend fields are missing

Does anyone know how to resolve this error message? I should also mention that I noticed almost the exact same question was posted here about a year ago, however in that circumstance the individual was able to resolve the issue by using ds() rather than ddf(), however because I know that I need to run an MCDS I don't think that solution will help here. Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks!
Nathaniel

messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Density estimation in R with multiple covariates
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Density estimation in R with multiple covariates
messages.body_plain:
Michelle

Sounds like a challenging dataset and you are trying to do a conscientious analysis.

First the easy question (1): "observer" is a reserved covariate name.  the ds() function sits on top of the machinery for doing mark-recapture distance sampling, where double observers are employed for the purposes of estimating g(0).  The simple solution is to rename that covariate "team" or some-such.

Harder question--measuring fit when the model being fitted has more parameters than points of support in the data.  No easy solution.  There is old literature on something called 'smearing' that essentially smooths through heaped detections (sect 7.4.3.4 of Buckland et al. (2001)).  However the methods for performing smearing are all ad-hoc, without a theoretical foundation.

Lastly, an unasked question: your description leads me to think that "team" and "year" are highly collinear (explaining similar sources of variation).  That will cause fitting problems and likely messy estimates of the parameters of the detection function.  First impressions are that using only "team" might be the way forward--assuming teams were spatial allocated so as not to mess spatial and team effects.

On 12/12/2016 18:13, Michelle Gibson wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I want to get density estimates for individual species from a multi-year bird survey (line transects), using year, observer, and cluster size as covariates as I have reason to believe that each might affect a species' detectability.  Ultimately, I would like to run the model: ds(data, ... , cutpoints = c(0,15,35,55,75,105,145), ... , formula = ~ as.factor(year) + as.factor(observer) + size).
>
> Year
> I think that year is affecting species' detectability because when I plotted detection function for each species with year as a covariate to see whether detection functions were different in each year and found that for many species the shape of the detection function was markedly different. However, this could be an artefact of having different observers in each year. I chose to use year as a covariate rather than doing full stratification by year (i.e. getting a separate detection function for each year) because the latter approach greatly limited the number of species with sufficient number observations (60 observations per stratum).
>
> Observer
> I have five years of data, and in each year two to three different teams conducted surveys, with essentially no overlap between teams in different years, giving 12 unique observer team IDs. Differences is observer effort and skill level can obviously lead to different biases in how species are detected, so I'd like to account for that.
>
> Cluster size
> I used cluster size as a covariate because I want to account for cluster-size bias (larger flock sizes are more likely to be detected at further distances).
>
> Problems:
>
> 1.) I am able to run ds models when my flatfile contains year as the only covariate (with columns 'Region.Label', 'Area', 'Sample.Label', 'Effort', 'distance', 'size', 'year', and 'species'). When I add an 'observer' column to my flatfile (with columns 'Region.Label', 'Area', 'Sample.Label', 'Effort', 'observer', 'distance', 'size', 'year', and 'species') and run the same model (with year as the only covariate), I get errors saying all models failed to fit/no models could be fitted. This tells me that adding an 'observer' column somehow messes up the flatfile and I cannot figure why this might be. I'd appreciate any ideas!
>
> 2.) Also, how should I assess model fit? I am using manually defined cutpoints/bins (6 in total) because of heaping of 'exact' distance estimates, and when year is used as a covariate there are 5 levels (2012-2016) so there are no remaining degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness of fit test.
>
> Thanks very much,
> Michelle
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Nathaniel

The software performing the maximum likelihood estimation of the detection function parameters differs between the GUI-software Distance and the R-based software; consequently for some complex (high number of parameter) models, the estimates will be slightly different.
Regarding debug mode and the existence of input files.  The files you describe "in.r", "ddf.dat.r", etc. are only created when Distance is using analysis engines such as MRDS or DSM; i.e. engines that use R software.  Your earlier message described your use of MCDS, which is written in Fortran rather than R, as a consequence, no ".r" files are created when MCDS analyses are run in debug mode.

If you are truly keen on making comparisons between MCDS results and results of similar models fit using R, I direct you to an experimental R package, "readdst" (available via github) that reads existing GUI-Distance projects, translates their data structures to R-type structures, and can perform estimation of analyses in the GUI-Distance project in R.  This package is a "work in progress" and requires some reasonable sophistication in the use of R.  There is a vignette describing its capabilities here
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/Project-migration.html
